A1.justification: Both PDFs describe ParticleGS and contain readable text, equations, figures, tables, and appendices. The substantial architectural and experimental revisions can be reliably compared.

before.justification: v1 reports original reconstruction and extrapolation experiments on synthetic datasets and PanopticSports, together with component ablations.

after.justification: v2 reports original benchmark results, component ablations, rendering-speed measurements, latent-state visualizations, and a spiral-dynamics toy experiment.

M1.justification: v2 replaces position-hash features and a max-pooled global state with Gaussian-attribute features and learnable-query attention over multiple dynamic fields. It revises the ODE architecture, replaces general affine/additive rotation updates with Rodrigues-based and quaternion updates, changes the stated loss weighting, and adds a separate dynamics warm-up. Periodic neighborhood rebuilding already existed in v1.

E1.justification: The Dynamic Object and Dynamic Indoor Scene datasets are retained. PanopticSports human-motion evaluation is removed, while Dynamic Multipart and FreeGave-GoPro add articulated-object motion and real-world human-object interactions. The appendix also adds a noisy 2D damped-oscillator experiment, extending coverage beyond video rendering.

E2.justification: On the retained synthetic benchmarks, v2 adds TRACE and FreeGave and removes 4D-GS from the quantitative comparisons. HexPlane, TiNeuVox, DeformGS, Grid4D, NVFi, and GaussianPrediction remain. These changes materially strengthen the velocity-field comparison and alter the comparator set independently of the added datasets.

E3.justification: Reported training budgets on the retained Object and Indoor datasets change from 50,000 and 60,000 iterations to 40,000, with a new dynamics warm-up between iterations 3,000 and 7,000. Their 75/25 temporal split is retained. v2 adds FPS evaluation and new ablation settings, including field-count sweeps and an A6000 exception to the otherwise RTX 4090 setup.

E4.justification: v1 Table 4 ablates latent space, Neural ODEs, and affine deformation. v2 substantially redesigns this analysis around factorized encoding, field count, ODE versus parameter-matched MLP, Rodrigues decoding, progressive training, and neighborhood rebuilding. Figure 3 adds latent-state analysis, and supplementary Section 6 adds a toy comparison of time-conditioned fitting against ODE extrapolation.

E5.justification: Neither version reports repeated-run or seed counts, confidence intervals, standard deviations, or statistical significance tests. Both primarily provide point estimates; the toy experiment's noisy inputs do not constitute uncertainty estimation.

E6.justification: ParticleGS extrapolation PSNR changes from 27.558 to 38.067 for Falling Ball and from 33.568 to 32.679 for Factory (v1 Tables 1–2; v2 Tables 5–6). These are revised-model and training-setting results, not controlled version-to-version gains. The six retained baselines keep their shared-dataset scene scores. New benchmark, speed, and ablation results are added, while PanopticSports results disappear.

T1.justification: v2 Section 3.2 adds the standard reduction of higher-order differential equations to an augmented first-order system, together with an explicit O(NG)-to-O(FG) evolution-complexity argument. These are bounded mathematical additions to v1's ODE formulation; no formal extrapolation or stability guarantee is established.

C1.justification: The broad claim of prior-free extrapolation from videos remains. However, v2 makes generalized higher-order dynamics beyond velocity-field models a central contribution and explicitly claims independence from geometric priors. It drops v1's categorical claim to be the first end-to-end general extrapolation method without manually defined physical priors.

C2.justification: v2 interprets performance through higher-order dynamics, shared-field efficiency, latent-state coherence, and the new training ablations. It replaces v1's emphasis on new-scene generalization and possible large-scale pretraining with a limitation concerning unseen changes in motion, such as breakage. v1's caution that rendering metrics can confound reconstruction quality with dynamics accuracy is also omitted.

D1.justification: Supplementary Section 7 specifies the 14-dimensional input, 2,048/4,096 sampled keypoints, 32 neighbors, latent dimensions, GELU activations, Adam optimizer, and detailed training stages. Network depths and widths are revised relative to v1 Appendix A.1. Conversely, v1's explicit code-availability statement and repository URL are removed; this establishes a disclosure loss, not that the repository became unavailable.

R1.justification: v2 substantially expands positioning against velocity-field methods and approaches requiring structured geometry, adding discussion and citations for TRACE, FreeGave, NeuMA, VisionLaw, and neural constitutive-law learning. v1 mainly contrasts reconstruction methods, imposed physical constraints, and GaussianPrediction. This revises the novelty argument beyond reference renumbering or publication updates.

P1.justification: The abstract, introduction, related work, methodology, and experimental discussion are extensively rewritten. The separate preliminaries are folded into the method formulation, and the appendix is reorganized into dedicated experimental, implementation, rotation-formula, visualization, and quantitative-results sections. The title and author information also change.

P2.justification: v2 switches to a two-column layout, redraws the introductory and architecture figures, and reorganizes qualitative comparisons with marked locations and enlarged details. It adds latent-state and spiral plots. Main-text NVFi scene tables become dataset summaries, with scene-level results relocated to the appendix; table highlighting changes from colored cells to bold and underlining.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens assessment of the central extrapolation claim: TRACE/FreeGave comparisons, targeted factorization and training ablations, and speed measurements address important gaps in v1's comparative and component evidence. More explicit architecture and implementation descriptions improve transparency. These gains outweigh the loss of PanopticSports coverage, code-access disclosure, and some qualifications. The improvement rests on stronger validation and documentation, not on treating revised scores as controlled gains or accepting physical-law identification as proven.
